title: Self-Diffusion of Water through Thermally Activated Membranes
abstract: Diffusion processes involving membranes are of fundamental importance in both science and technology, since membranes serve as selective interfaces that regulate the transport of mass, charge, and information across multiple length and time scales. In this study, we employ molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to calculate the self-diffusion coefficient, tetrahedral order parameter and hydrogen-bond (HB) lifetime of SPC/E water over a wide high-temperature range in the presence of thermally activated membranes (TAMs). These membranes exhibit thermally controlled stochastic behavior that locally influences particle dynamics by probabilistically inducing elastic scattering events as particles traverse the membrane. The stochastic behavior of the membranes is governed by a sigmoidal profile, which depend on the reduced temperature of the system. The effective activation energy for diffusion is estimated for several membrane configurations. It is found that the diffusion coefficients generally decrease with an increase in the number of membranes and are in reasonable agreement with the Arrhenius approximation at high temperatures. Additionally, both the tetrahedral order parameter and the HB lifetime are only locally sensitive to the action of the membranes.
summary: This work uses Molecular Dynamics simulations to study how water diffuses through membranes that introduce stochastic scattering events. The research finds that while the membranes significantly impede bulk diffusion, they have only a minor effect on the local structural order or the lifetime of hydrogen bonds. This highlights a decoupling between macroscopic transport and local molecular structure.
main_problem: The study investigates how the self-diffusion of water is altered when passing through Thermally Activated Membranes (TAMs). It aims to understand the influence of these stochastic interfaces on particle dynamics and hydrogen-bond structure.
main_result: TAMs significantly decrease the self-diffusion coefficient as the number of membranes increases, but they only exert a weak influence on the local tetrahedral order parameter and hydrogen-bond lifetime.
method: Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations are employed to track particle trajectories and calculate various thermodynamic and structural properties over a range of temperatures.
model_or_system: The system uses the SPC/E water model confined in a cubic domain containing planar TAMs. The membrane interaction is modeled stochastically, inducing elastic scattering events governed by a temperature-dependent sigmoidal probability.
key_observables: Self-diffusion coefficient (D), tetrahedral order parameter ($\langle q angle$), Hydrogen-bond (HB) lifetime ($	au_{HB}$), and effective activation energy ($E_a$).
important_parameters: Temperature (T), membrane configuration (number of TAMs, W), and reduced temperature ($	heta = T/T_0$).
main_assumptions: The membrane interaction is modeled as a probabilistic, elastic scattering event; the system dynamics are analyzed using MD simulations.
figures_summary: Figures show MSD vs. time for diffusion coefficient calculation, $\langle q angle$ vs. T for structure, and $	au_{HB}$ vs. T for dynamics, comparing membrane presence (W=0 vs W=3).
paper_structure: The paper systematically calculates diffusion coefficients, structural parameters ($\langle q angle$), and HB lifetimes across different membrane configurations and temperatures, comparing results to established theoretical approximations like the Arrhenius law.
why_interesting: The study models non-equilibrium transport phenomena in a complex fluid system, providing insights into how imposed boundaries or interfaces (like membranes) modify fundamental transport coefficients, which is relevant to open quantum systems and energy dissipation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The schematic depicts a three-dimensional simulation box with periodic boundary conditions containing N = 103 water molecules. A single thermoactivated membrane (rendered in trans- parent blue) is positioned at the center of the box.

Figure 2: Plot of the MSD as a function of time at temperature T = 387.3 K and density ρ = 1.0 g/cm3 for two diﬀerent W-membrane conﬁgurations (see Sec. 3). The self-diﬀusion coeﬃcient, D, is deter- mined from the slope of the MSD according to Eq. (18). The asymp- totic diﬀusion coeﬃcient is obtained by performing a least-squares linear ﬁt to the long-time regime (red solid lines), over the time inter- val from 30τ to 50τ (black dashed lines). Similar plots are obtained for the other temperatures and densities investigated. The scaling pa- rameters σ and τ are listed in Table 1.

Figure 3: Semi-log plot of the self-diﬀusion coeﬃcients (in physical units) as a function of temperature for the diﬀerent TAM conﬁgurations and the two water-density regimes. The Arrhenius curve ﬁtted to data are also shown (solid lines) and the respective activation energies (Ea) and pre-exponential factor (D0) are reported in Table 2. Error bars are of the same size of plot symbols and are not showed. (a) Absence of TAMs (W = 0). (b) Presence of a single TAM (W = 1). (c) Presence of two TAMs (W = 2). (d) Presence of three TAMs (W = 3).

Figure 4: Tetrahedrality distribution, P(q), and the mean tetrahedrality, ⟨q⟩(see the plot legends), at temperatures (a) T = 310, K and (b) T = 387, K for the two W cases considered, at a water density of 1.0 g/cm3. According to Eq. (13), at T = 310 K, the probability that a given water molecule undergoes elastic scattering at the membrane is p ≃0.52, whereas at T = 387 K, this probability increases to p ≃0.75.

Figure 5: Mean tetrahedrality, ⟨q⟩, calculated for water molecules within virtual boxes of diﬀerent lengths centered at the membrane (x = 0), at (a) T = 310, K and (b) T = 387, K, for a water density of 1.0 g/cm3. Results are shown for two diﬀerent W cases, with the virtual-box length ranging from L/32 to L/2 (L = 9.8 σ).
